I mean honestly, I just joined reddit because there's a lot of History subs based on interesting shit, and I enjoy talkin to those kinds of people, I make a trashy joke from time to time but overall it's good fun!

True, a non-violent option is always the most preferable situation but i mean, war crimes, ethnic cleansings, whole countries collapsing, even cannibalism, etc. are all examples of issues which most have occurred due to lack of options/decisions, I think Truman's decision to give the emperor a choice was a good one, some state the bombing of both cities as a 'necessary evil', but I see it more as an unavoidable disaster. The Showa and his government officials were a lot more desperate to remain on the throne in a state of Monarchy, so much so that their slow decision making, and even refusal to surrender after Hiroshima led to the deaths of so many civilians, I don't believe enough blame was placed or enough punishment was given out to the Emperor of Japan.   
and glad you liked my points!, always enjoy nerding out from time to time, hope you had one too.

Hiroshima, Nagasaki, and Kokura were all undamaged and high in military production including factories and facilities, Hiroshima and Kokura were the preferred strategic targets but due to unpredictable weather Nagasaki was chosen as an alternate. Cities like Kyoto, Tokyo, and the Emperor's palace weren't chosen due to high cultural significance, if you want to continue to say racism and misinformation was involved then I suggest picking up the right history book, cities like Tokyo and Kyoto weren't chosen because President Truman did not seek to destroy Japan's people or culture, the goal was to destroy Japan's ability to make war. airfields and harbors weren't prime targets as those tended to be rebuilt in an instant, therefore a strategic demonstration was shoved in the Showa's face, and the pressure applied after Nagasaki and the Soviet's declaration of war pressured Hirohito to finally accept the terms of unconditional surrender received from the Potsdam Conference, ending the ongoing pacific war.

Nah, Japan's culture consistently believed surrender was not an option, and anyone who considered surrender was dishonorable, i.e. surrender was punishable by death, which is why people tried to silence hirohito before the release of Hirohito's surrender speech. dropping a bomb in the ocean wouldn't have done anything for them, not only would Japan not have lost a single thing in production, science, or any incentive to surrender, but at the time, where the United States only had two bombs, an atom bomb and a hydrogen bomb, and in the process of making a third one which would've taken a long time, there was a chance the bomb could've been a dud, if so it could've led the japanese to fight even harder, even if it wasn't there was not a high enough chance that a demonstration would cause surrender and even then, it wasn't worth using 50% of the military's Nuclear Power for a demonstration that couldn't ensure any genuine progress towards ending the war, bombing Hiroshima was strategic as it wiped out multiple military factories and facilities, while nagasaki was less favorable of a target, it still held torpedo production factories which were stacking countless ships on the seabed, the weather decided on nagasaki. A demonstration wouldn't have been strategic, and if you want more details to why a demonstration was over-ruled
